Learning Objectives The assignment should help students learn: - How an HTML parser works at a basic level - How a DOM is represented as a tree - Tree data structures - Recursion - Strings and parsing - File handling - Command-line arguments - Error handling - Dynamic memory and pointers in C - Classes and data structures in Python - Software modularity - Testing - Debugging - Git-based development - AI-assisted programming with OpenCode - Preserving engineering context using Entire - The difference between generating code and engineering software --- # 3. Problem Statement Given an HTML file such as: ```html <html> <body> <h1>Hello</h1> <p>Welcome to AI Karyashala</p> </body> </html> ``` the application must: 1. Read the HTML file. 2. Parse the HTML. 3. Construct an in-memory DOM tree. 4. Traverse the DOM tree. 5. Display the DOM tree in a format similar to the Linux `tree` command. The output should look like: ```text . └── html └── body ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── p └── "Welcome to AI Karyashala" ``` The important requirement is that the tree output must be generated by **traversing the in-memory DOM**, not by simply formatting the original HTML. --- # 4. Scope of HTML Do NOT require students to implement the complete HTML5 specification. Define a small, clear subset of HTML. The parser should initially support: - Opening tags - Closing tags - Text nodes - Nested elements - Sibling elements - Attributes - Whitespace between elements For example: ```html <div> <h1>Hello</h1> <p class="intro">Welcome</p> </div> ``` The parser should create a tree containing: ```text div ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── p [class="intro"] └── "Welcome" ``` Clearly state which HTML features are **out of scope**, such as: - JavaScript - CSS parsing - HTML entities - Browser rendering - Complete HTML5 error recovery - Comments, unless introduced as an optional extension - DOCTYPE processing, unless introduced as an optional extension - Script/style parsing --- # 5. DOM Data Model Require students to design an internal representation for the DOM. At minimum, the DOM should represent: ### Element Node - Tag name - Attributes - Children ### Text Node - Text content Explain that the exact implementation is left to the student. For example, in C they may use structures, pointers, linked lists, or dynamic arrays. In Python they may use classes, lists, dictionaries, or other suitable structures. Do not prescribe the implementation unnecessarily. --- # 6. Tree Output Requirement This is an important part of the assignment. The DOM must be displayed like the Unix `tree` command. Use: ```text ├── └── │ ``` appropriately. Example: ```text . └── html └── body ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── p └── "Welcome to AI Karyashala" ``` For attributes: ```text . └── html └── body ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── p [class="intro", id="first"] └── "Welcome to AI Karyashala" ``` Text nodes must be displayed inside quotation marks. The tree printer must be implemented by recursively traversing the DOM data structure. --- # 7. CLI Interface Define a simple command-line interface. For example: ```text domparser page.html ``` should display the DOM tree. Also introduce useful options: ```text domparser page.html --tree domparser page.html --text domparser page.html --tags p domparser page.html --find-id first domparser page.html --find-class intro ``` The exact command name can be chosen by the students, but the behavior must be documented. --- # 8. Development Phases Structure the assignment into incremental milestones. ## Phase 1 — Read HTML - Read an HTML file. - Display its contents. - Understand the input. ## Phase 2 — Tokenization / Parsing - Identify opening tags. - Identify closing tags. - Identify text. ## Phase 3 — Build DOM - Create the DOM node representation. - Build parent-child relationships. - Support nested elements. ## Phase 4 — Tree Display Traverse the DOM recursively and produce the `tree`-style output. ## Phase 5 — Attributes Support attributes such as: ```html <p class="intro" id="first">Hello</p> ``` ## Phase 6 — Validation Detect basic malformed HTML. Examples: ```text Unclosed tag: <p> Unexpected closing tag: </div> ``` ## Phase 7 — Queries Add simple DOM queries: ```text --find-tag p --find-id first --find-class intro ``` ## Phase 8 — Testing and Refactoring Create tests for: - Simple elements - Nested elements - Multiple siblings - Text nodes - Attributes - Empty elements - Malformed HTML - Deeply nested HTML --- # 9. C Implementation The C version should give students practice with: - `struct` - Pointers - Dynamic memory allocation - Strings - Arrays or linked lists - Tree structures - Recursion - File I/O - Command-line arguments - Error handling Do not provide the implementation. The students must design and implement the data structures themselves. --- # 10. Python Implementation The Python version should give students practice with: - Classes - Objects - Lists - Dictionaries - Strings - File handling - Exceptions - Recursion - Command-line arguments - Modular programming Again, do not provide the implementation. --- # 11. OpenCode Requirement OpenCode must be an explicit part of the assignment. Students must NOT simply ask: > "Build the complete HTML parser for me." Instead, require them to use an iterative engineering workflow. For example: ```text Problem ↓ Understand ↓ Plan ↓ Design ↓ Implement ↓ Run ↓ Test ↓ Debug ↓ Refactor ↓ Commit ``` Students should use OpenCode to: - Understand requirements - Discuss design alternatives - Create an implementation plan - Implement individual features - Generate tests - Diagnose errors - Refactor code - Review their implementation Require them to keep a record of important prompts and AI decisions. --- # 12. Entire Requirement Students must use Entire during development. The assignment should explain that the purpose is to preserve development context beyond the final source code. Students should examine what Entire records about: - Development sessions - Intent - Decisions - Changes - AI-assisted development - Reasoning/context around changes Students should be asked to compare: **Git alone** versus **Git + development context captured by Entire** The assignment should not prescribe exactly what Entire must capture; students should discover this through actual use. --- # 13. Git Requirements Each implementation must use Git. Require at least **5 meaningful commits**. Do not accept meaningless commits such as: ```text update changes final done ``` Examples of meaningful commits: ```text Create DOM node representation Implement basic HTML parser Add recursive tree printer Add attribute parsing Add malformed HTML detection Add DOM query support ``` Students should be able to explain what changed in each important commit. --- # 14. Two Implementations Students must create: ```text dom-parser-c/ dom-parser-python/ ``` Both implementations must support the same input and produce equivalent DOM tree output. The goal is NOT to copy the C implementation into Python. Students should make appropriate language-specific design decisions. --- # 15. Sample Input Files Create several sample HTML files for the assignment. ### simple.html ```html <html> <body> <h1>Hello</h1> </body> </html> ``` ### nested.html ```html <div> <section> <h1>Title</h1> <p>Hello</p> </section> </div> ``` ### attributes.html ```html <div id="main" class="container"> <p class="intro">Hello</p> <p>World</p> </div> ``` ### siblings.html ```html <ul> <li>One</li> <li>Two</li> <li>Three</li> </ul> ``` ### malformed.html Provide examples containing: - Missing closing tags - Unexpected closing tags - Incorrect nesting --- # 16. Expected Output For each sample input, provide expected tree-style output. Make the examples sufficiently clear that students can test their programs against them. --- # 17. Testing Require students to create automated tests where appropriate. Tests should cover: - Parsing - DOM construction - Tree traversal - Attributes - Text nodes - Error detection - Queries Also require students to perform manual CLI testing. --- # 18. Final Comparison Students must compare the two implementations. Require them to answer questions such as: 1. Which implementation was easier to develop? 2. Why? 3. How did memory management affect the C implementation? 4. What did Python make easier? 5. What was difficult for the AI agent? 6. Where did the AI generate incorrect or poor code? 7. How did they verify AI-generated code? 8. What design decisions did they make themselves? 9. How did OpenCode change their development workflow? 10. What did Entire preserve that Git alone did not? 11. What would another developer need to understand the project six months later? 12. Is source code alone a complete record of software development when AI agents are involved? --- # 19. Final Deliverables Each student must submit: ```text project/ ├── c/ ├── python/ ├── tests/ ├── samples/ ├── README.md └── development-notes/ ``` The exact structure may be adjusted by the student. The repository must contain: - C implementation - Python implementation - Sample HTML files - Tests - README - Git history - OpenCode development evidence - Entire development context - Final comparison/reflection --- # 20. Evaluation Rubric Create a clear rubric totaling 100 marks. Include categories such as: - DOM design — 15 - HTML parsing — 15 - Tree construction — 15 - Tree-style output — 10 - Attributes and queries — 10 - Error handling — 10 - Testing — 10 - C implementation quality — 5 - Python implementation quality — 5 - OpenCode usage — 3 - Entire usage — 2 Adjust the distribution if necessary, but make **actual engineering quality** more important than simply completing features. --- # 21. Important Rules Include these rules prominently: 1. Do not use an existing HTML/DOM parser library. 2. Do not copy an implementation from the Internet. 3. AI-generated code must be understood and verified. 4. Students must be able to explain their own implementation. 5. OpenCode is a development assistant, not a substitute for understanding. 6. Git commits must reflect actual development. 7. Entire must be used throughout development, not added at the end. 8. C and Python implementations must be independently developed. --- # 22. Final Reflection End the assignment with a reflection section titled: **What Does Software Engineering Look Like When AI Writes Code?** Ask students to write a short reflection addressing: > If an AI coding agent can generate a large portion of the source code, what becomes more important for a software engineer? Include prompts around: - Problem understanding - System design - Decomposition - Asking good questions - Verification - Testing - Debugging - Reviewing AI output - Making engineering decisions - Preserving development context --- ## Output expected from you Create the complete assignment as a polished, student-ready document. Do not implement the parser. Do not provide the solution. Do not provide C or Python source code. # OpenCode Quick Start Guide

## Linux Installation
The recommended approach is using the install script:
```bash
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
```

Alternatively, install via Homebrew: `brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode`

## Starting in a Project
Navigate to your project directory and launch OpenCode:
```bash
cd /path/to/project
opencode
```

## Connecting a Model Provider
Run the `/connect` command within OpenCode's interface. The documentation recommends trying "OpenCode Zen" for curated, tested models if you're new to LLM providers. You'll need to obtain an API key from your chosen provider and paste it when prompted.

## Project Initialization
Execute `/init` to have OpenCode analyze your project structure and generate an `AGENTS.md` file in the root directory. This file should be committed to Git, as it helps OpenCode understand "the project structure and the coding patterns used."

## Plan vs. Build Modes
OpenCode offers two operational modes toggled via the **Tab** key:

- **Plan Mode**: Disables direct code modifications; instead, it "suggest[s] _how_ it'll implement the feature"
- **Build Mode**: Enables OpenCode to make actual code changes

Start in Plan mode to review the proposed approach before switching to Build mode to execute changes.

# Build a Mini HTML Parser — Quiz A quick check of the basics before (and during) the assignment. Try each question first, **then** click **Show answer** to check yourself. Read the reason, not just the letter. --- ## OpenCode **1. OpenCode has a Plan mode and a Build mode. What is the difference?** - A. Plan mode is faster; Build mode is more accurate - B. Plan mode only discusses and proposes; Build mode is allowed to change your files - C. Plan mode writes the tests; Build mode writes the code - D. There is no difference; they are two names for the same mode
Show answer **B.** In Plan mode the agent can read your project and suggest *how* it would do something, but it does not edit your files. Build mode lets it make the changes. Plan first, read the plan, *then* build — that is how you stay in charge of the design.
**2. What is the `AGENTS.md` file that OpenCode can generate for a project?** - A. A list of every person who worked on the project - B. A log of every prompt you have typed - C. A description of the project — its structure and conventions — that the agent reads to understand it - D. A licence file
Show answer **C.** `AGENTS.md` tells the agent what this project is and how its code is organised. It belongs in Git with your code. The agent writes a first version, but **you** should read it and correct anything wrong — a wrong `AGENTS.md` misleads every later session.
**3. Which prompt is the better one to give OpenCode in Phase 5?** - A. `make the parser better` - B. `finish the assignment` - C. `Add attribute parsing: store each name="value" pair on the element in source order, and print them as [name="value", ...]. Don't change the tree printer's branch logic.` - D. `fix everything`
Show answer **C.** It names **one** feature, says exactly what correct looks like, and says what must **not** change. The others give the agent no way to know when it is done — so it guesses, and you get code you did not design.
**4. OpenCode writes a test, and the test passes. What must you still check?**
Show answer That the test's **expected output is actually right**. If the agent misunderstood the rules, it can write wrong code *and* a test that expects the same wrong answer — and it will pass. Work out the expected output by hand (or compare with the sample files in the assignment) before you trust the test.
--- ## Entire **5. In Entire, what is a checkpoint?** - A. A backup copy of your whole hard disk - B. A Git branch for each new feature - C. A code change linked to the agent session behind it — the prompt, the conversation, and the tool calls - D. A test that must pass before you can commit
Show answer **C.** A checkpoint pairs **what changed** (your commit) with **why and how it changed** (the agent session). That pairing is the whole point: Git alone has the first half only.
**6. Where does Entire keep the checkpoint data?** - A. Inside your source files, as comments - B. In your own Git repository, but separate from your source branches - C. In your commit messages - D. Only in the browser, never on your machine
Show answer **B.** Checkpoints live in your own repository, stored apart from your normal branches, so your code history stays clean and the context travels with the repository when you push. You can also browse them on entire.io.
**7. Why must Entire be enabled from the first commit, not at the end?**
Show answer Entire can only record sessions **while they happen**. Turn it on at the end and every earlier decision, wrong attempt, and reason is already gone — you would have checkpoints only for the last few commits, the least interesting ones.
**8. Fill in the blanks:** Git records **______** changed. Entire also records **______** it changed — the prompt and the conversation behind the change.
Show answer Git records **what** changed. Entire also records **why** (and how) it changed. A diff shows the new line; it cannot show the three alternatives you rejected before choosing it.
--- ## Git and GitHub **9. Which of these are meaningful commit messages?** 1. `update` 2. `Add recursive tree printer` 3. `final` 4. `Detect unexpected closing tags` 5. `changes`
Show answer **2 and 4.** Each says what changed, in a few words, in the imperative. `update`, `final`, and `changes` would fit *any* commit in *any* project — so they tell a reader nothing.
**10. Why commit at the end of every phase instead of once at the end?**
Show answer Small commits make the history tell the story of how the program grew, let you go back to the last working state when something breaks, and give Entire a checkpoint per step — so each piece of context sits next to the change it explains.
--- ## The parser **11. Your program prints exactly the right tree for every sample, but it never builds a tree — it just re-indents the HTML text. Does it meet the requirement?**
Show answer **No.** The output must come from **walking a DOM tree in memory**. Re-indenting text can match the samples and still have no tree to query (`--find-class` needs one) and nothing to validate against. Right output from the wrong method still fails.
**12. While parsing, you keep a list of the elements that are open right now. A closing tag arrives. Which open element is the only one it may close?**
Show answer The **innermost** one — the one opened most recently. That is why a **stack** (last in, first out) fits: push on an opening tag, pop on a matching closing tag. In `Bold italic`, `` arrives while `` is innermost — so it is an error: `Unexpected closing tag: (expected )`.

  1. Read
  2. Write
```
